 Singaporean Extradited To US Over Alleged Global Insider-Trading Scheme Worth Millions
 Global
 Extradition brings alleged global insider-trading network before US court.
 Extradition brings alleged global insider-trading network before US court.

 A Singaporean man has been extradited to the United States to face charges over an alleged international insider-trading network that prosecutors say generated tens of millions of dollars through confidential corporate information.
 Zhi Ge, 35, appeared before a federal court in Boston on Friday, November 20, following his extradition from Singapore, according to the US Department of Justice.
 He faces securities fraud and money-laundering charges over allegations that he helped lead a network involved in trading shares using non-public information about companies’ financial performance and planned mergers.
 Ge is among nine individuals accused of participating in the alleged scheme, which prosecutors say operated between 2016 and 2024.
 The indictment alleges that the network relied on information supplied by investment bankers and other corporate insiders who had access to sensitive details before they were made public.
 Prosecutors say Ge worked alongside Samy Khouadja, a former investment banker in France, and Eamma Safi, who co-owned a restaurant with Khouadja.
 The group allegedly recruited people with access to confidential business information and paid them in exchange for tips that could be used to make profitable trades before major corporate announcements.

 Among the transactions identified in the court documents were deals involving pharmaceutical companies AstraZeneca and Novartis.
 Prosecutors allege that the information was used to trade ahead of AstraZeneca’s planned $39 billion acquisition of Alexion Pharmaceuticals in 2020 and Novartis’ acquisition of MorphoSys in 2024.
 The indictment also claims that members of the network used burner phones, encrypted messaging applications and coded language to conceal their activities and avoid detection.
 Investigators allege that the group used expressions such as “greens” when referring to money and other coded terms when discussing potential merger partners.
 The case also involves allegations that confidential information was shared with journalists to generate additional trading opportunities once the information became public.
 Ge was arrested in Singapore in 2024, and a court there recently ordered his extradition to the United States.
 His lawyer, Kevin Barron, said his client would plead not guilty and intended to vigorously defend himself. Ge is scheduled to return to federal court on December 16.
 The case highlights the international reach of financial crime investigations and the challenges regulators face when confidential market information is allegedly passed across borders.
 The allegations have not been proven in court, and the defendants are entitled to the presumption of innocence.
 Catherine Okonkwo
